title: Product-based planning with story maps
blurb: Explain how PRINCE2 product-based planning works in agile, with a user story map in place of the product breakdown structure and releases clustered across it.
question: An agile team wants to break its products down for planning without drawing a separate product breakdown structure. Which artifact does PRINCE2 Agile recommend, and what does it feed?

teach.body: The plans practice defines the products (what) and the means (who, how and where), with estimates of when and how much, to satisfy the business case (why). PRINCE2 Agile keeps this product focus. Its version of product-based planning still starts from what must be delivered, but uses agile artifacts to break products down and group them into releases.

head: PRINCE2 output
PRINCE2 Agile form
rows: Defined while building the release map

teach.h: The story map replaces the PBS
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map. Story mapping is a technique for defining and breaking down the work needed to build a product that meets user needs. As the map is built, products are broken into smaller user stories, so a separate product breakdown document is no longer needed. The story map is a plans practice artifact.

teach.h: A story map sliced into releases
From story map to release map
teach.body: The release map is built from the story map: user stories are clustered into releases that make sense from a priority and a development or technical point of view. Each release is visually separated and given a deadline, usually two to four iterations away. Turning the story map into a release map is also when dependencies between products are defined, so releases can be planned around them.

teach.h: Product breakdown structure versus story map
The rest of the planning still happens
teach.body: Breaking products down is not the whole job. Estimates are still prepared, and the budget step covers the cost of producing and delivering the products (people, equipment, materials and facilities) plus the cost of project management activities. The release map then carries or refers to the budget, tolerances and assumptions.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3.1.5 and Table 8.1

teach.h: Worked scenario: Fenwick Valley Leisure Trust
teach.body: The trust is building an online swimming-lesson booking service. Project manager Tomasz Wilk and chief product owner Grace Adeyemi run a story-mapping session using two personas, a busy parent and a swimming teacher. The team lists user activities in order, from finding a class to getting reminders, and writes stories under each. They draw a line across the map: everything above it becomes release 1. Card payment must be set up before booking can go live, so that dependency shapes the release map.

teach.text: The story map replaces the product breakdown structure, not the project plan: the plan is the release map built from it. The story map is a plans artifact, not part of the business case (project canvas) or the quality practice (Definition of Ready).

items: Product-based planning still starts from products in PRINCE2 Agile (8.3.1).
A user story map is recommended in place of the product breakdown structure.
Story mapping: personas, user activities in time order, then user stories.
Stories are clustered into releases by priority and development sense.
Turning the story map into a release map also defines dependencies.
The budget covers product costs plus project management costs.

summary: You can now explain how product-based planning works in PRINCE2 Agile, with a user story map in place of the product breakdown structure. You can also describe how stories on the map are clustered into releases to form the release map.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, which artifact is recommended to replace the product breakdown structure?
A.why: The book recommends replacing the PBS with a user story map, which breaks products into user stories (8.3.1.1, 8.3.2.4).

whyNot.0: The release map is the plan built from the story map, not the replacement for the PBS.
whyNot.1: The product flow diagram shows sequence and dependencies; it is not a breakdown of products.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is the business case artifact, not a breakdown of products.

A.q: Where does a team usually start when building a story map?
A.why: The team starts with user descriptions or personas and brainstorms the activities those users want to perform (8.3.2.4).

whyNot.1: Budget and tolerances belong in or alongside the release map, later in planning.
whyNot.2: The skill matrix maps team capabilities in the organization practice.
whyNot.3: The risk register records risks; it is not the starting point for mapping user needs.

A.q: Which artifact provides the information used to create a release map?
A.why: A release map is created from the story map by clustering user stories into suitable releases (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: The team dashboard shows team progress; it replaces the checkpoint report.
whyNot.1: The delegation matrix shows who decides what; it does not feed release planning.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities and results.

B.q: Which step of the product-based planning technique does story mapping represent in PRINCE2 Agile?
B.why: The story map represents the 'create a product breakdown structure' step; products are broken into user stories on the map (8.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: The project product description is tailored into the project backlog, not the story map.
whyNot.2: Scheduling follows later; releases are given dates on the release map.
whyNot.3: Documenting the plan produces the release map with its budget, tolerances and assumptions.

B.q:
Which two statements about story maps are correct?
1. User activities are ordered chronologically on the map.
2. The story map replaces the project canvas.
3. Turning a story map into a release map also defines dependencies.
4. The story map is an artifact of the quality practice.
B.why: Activities are ordered in time (8.3.2.4), and dependencies are defined while turning the story map into a release map (8.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: the project canvas is the business case artifact.
whyNot.2: Both are false: the story map belongs to the plans practice and does not replace the canvas.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the story map is a plans practice artifact.

B.q: When user stories from a story map are clustered into releases, each release should make sense from which points of view?
B.why: Stories are clustered into releases that make sense from a priority and a development or technical point of view (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: Costs and contracts are covered by the budget and the commercial management approach, not release clustering.
whyNot.1: Risk appetite and audit are governance concerns, not the basis for grouping stories.
whyNot.2: Staffing and location relate to team structure, not to how stories form releases.

C.q: To which practice does the story map belong, and which artifact does it feed?
C.why: Story mapping is a plans practice technique, and its stories are clustered into releases on the release map (8.3.2.4, 8.3.2.5).

whyNot.1: The product register tracks product status in the quality practice; it is not built from the story map.
whyNot.2: The project canvas is the business case artifact; the story map is a plans artifact.
whyNot.3: The practice is right, but the team dashboard reports team progress rather than being built from the map.

C.q: A team builds a story map. Does it also need a separate product breakdown structure, and why?
options: Yes, because the board must approve a PBS
Yes, because the PBS replaces the product backlog
No, because the map breaks products into stories
No, because the release map lists every task
C.why: During story mapping, products are broken into smaller user stories, removing the need for a separate product breakdown document (8.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: The board approves plans such as the release map; there is no rule that it must approve a PBS.
whyNot.1: The product backlog replaces product descriptions; a PBS does not replace it.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the release map is high level, not a task list.

C.q: When the budget is prepared in PRINCE2 Agile product-based planning, what does it cover?
options: Delivery team costs, with project management excluded
The supplier's price for the first iteration
The next iteration, with later work excluded
Costs of producing the products and of project management
C.why: The budget step covers the costs of producing and delivering the products (people, equipment, materials, facilities) and the cost of project management activities (8.3.1.5).

whyNot.0: Project management activity costs are included, not excluded.
whyNot.1: A single iteration's supplier price is far narrower than the project budget.
whyNot.2: The budget covers the plan's horizon, not one iteration.

reteach.title: Map the journey, then cut it into trips
reteach.question: If you planned a long holiday, would you list every item in your suitcase first, or sketch the journey day by day and decide what you need for each leg?

blocks.h: A map of what users do
blocks.body: A story map lays out what users do, in the order they do it, with smaller stories underneath. That breakdown is the agile replacement for a product breakdown structure. Draw lines across it and each band becomes a release: the most valuable, technically sensible stories go first.

blocks.text: The story map is the breakdown; the release map is the plan. Do not mix up the two maps.

explain.body: The plans practice defines the products (what) and the means (who, how, where), with when and how much, to satisfy the business case (why).

test.q: When the plans practice defines the products, which question is it answering?
test.why: Plans define the products (what) and the means to deliver them (8.1).

whyNot.0: Why the project exists is answered by the business case.
whyNot.2: What-if questions about uncertainty belong to the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Accountability is defined by the organization practice.

explain.h: Story map in place of the PBS
explain.body: Story mapping breaks products into user stories, so a separate product breakdown structure is not needed.

test.q: A team breaks its products into user stories on a story map. Which planning output does this make unnecessary?
test.why: The PBS is recommended to be replaced by the story map, removing the need for a separate breakdown document (8.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: The release map is still needed: it is built from the story map.
whyNot.1: The project backlog replaces the project product description and is still needed.
whyNot.3: Work package descriptions, as sets of user stories, are still agreed between PM and PO.

explain.body: Start from personas, brainstorm user activities, put them in chronological order, then break each into user stories.

test.q: After brainstorming user activities, what does the team do next when building a story map?
options: Cost each one in the budget
Log each one as a risk
test.why: Activities are organized in chronological order before being broken into stories (8.3.2.4).

whyNot.1: Allocation of work happens later, through work packages and team planning.
whyNot.2: Costing belongs to the budget step, not to building the map.
whyNot.3: Activities are user needs, not risks.

explain.body: Stories are clustered into releases by priority and development sense. Each release is given a deadline, usually two to four iterations.

test.q: How many iterations does a release usually contain?
test.why: Releases are given deadlines that usually contain two to four iterations (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: A single iteration is the smallest timebox, not a typical release.
whyNot.2: Five to eight is longer than the usual release length.
whyNot.3: Ten or more would be far longer than the usual release.
